div.p: Autonomous AI agents built on open-source runtimes such as OpenClaw expose every available tool to every session by default, regardless of the task at hand. A summarisation task receives the same shell execution, subagent spawning, and credential-access capabilities as a code deployment task -a 15× over-provision ratio we term the capability overprovisioning problem. Existing defenses (Nemo-Claw's container sandbox, Cisco DefenseClaw's skill scanner) address containment and threat detection, but neither learns the minimum viable capability set for each task type. We present AgentWarden, a three-layer adaptive governance framework that enforces the principle of least privilege for AI agents via a learned policy. Layer 1 (Capability Governor) dynamically scopes which tools the agent is aware of per session. Layer 3 (Safety Router) intercepts every tool call before execution using a hybrid rule-based and fine-tuned LLM classifier. Layer 2 (RL Learning Policy) trains a PPO policy on the accumulated audit log to learn the minimum viable skill set per task type. On a live OpenClaw v2026.3.28 deployment with DeepSeek-chat as the agent LLM, AgentWarden achieves: (i) 73% tool reduction and 100% dangerous tool elimination for summarisation tasks; (ii) a Skill Economy Ratio improvement of +260% (synthetic) and +337% (real sessions) over the uncontrolled baseline after PPO training (<5 minutes, RTX 3090); (iii) across an automated N=500 evaluation (400 benign + 100 adversarial, seed=42), 26.2% of all 447 intercepted tool calls were blocked, exec and sessions spawn were blocked at 100%, and 92% of adversarial tasks were neutralised by the model-plus-infrastructure stack. The evaluation dataset (N=500, seed=42) and trained artifacts are available upon request at https://github.com/sidikbro/agentwarden-core/.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The rapid adoption of autonomous AI agents has outpaced the security infrastructure designed to govern them. OpenClaw OpenClaw Contributors [2026], the dominant open-source personal AI agent runtime with over 500,000 internet-facing instances VentureBeat [2026], exposes a fixed set of 15+ tools to every session, regardless of the task being performed. An agent asked to summarize a document receives the same shell execution (exec), subagent spawning (sessions spawn), and credential-access capabilities as an agent performing infrastructure automation. We quantify this as a 15× over-provision ratio for summarization tasks. This over-provisioning has concrete security consequences. The ClawHavoc supply chain attack CrowdStrike Intelligence [2026] exploited OpenClaw's unrestricted tool access to distribute infostealers across 20% of ClawHub's skill registry. CVE-2026-25253 demonstrated that a single malicious webpage could hijack an agent's full capability set via prompt injection NVD [2026]. The attack surface is the agent's own capability scope.
The capability over-provisioning problem has a precise formulation: for a given task type τ , the Skill Economy Ratio (SER) measures the fraction of exposed tools that the agent actually invokes:

An ideal governance system achieves SER≈ 1.0 -the agent has access to exactly the tools it needs and nothing more. The OpenClaw baseline achieves SER= 0.067 for summarization (1 tool used of 15 exposed).

Existing defenses are incomplete. NVIDIA NemoClaw NVIDIA [2026] provides container-level sandboxing with declarative YAML policies -a static firewall that applies the same rules regardless of task type. Cisco DefenseClaw Cisco AI Defense [2026] scans skills for known malicious patterns and monitors runtime behavior anomalies -a reactive WAF that acts after the agent has decided to use a tool. Neither system learns the minimum capability set for each task type, and neither reduces the agent's awareness of capabilities it should not have.

Our contribution is AgentWarden, a four-layer governance framework that treats capability scoping as a learned optimization problem rather than a static configuration problem. The key insight is that an agent cannot misuse a tool it does not know exists. By dynamically restricting the agent's capability awareness via AGENTS.md injection (Layer 1) and learning the optimal restriction policy via PPO reinforcement learning (Layer 2), AgentWarden provides infrastructure-level governance that improves over time.
Scope. This work addresses capability governance -which tools an agent may invoke. Semantic output filtering (governing what the agent says) is orthogonal and out of scope.

Relationship to NemoClaw and DefenseClaw. We position AgentWarden as complementary rather than competing. NemoClaw asks "can the agent reach the outside world?" DefenseClaw asks "did this skill do something bad?" AgentWarden asks "why does the agent even know it has exec during a summarization task?" All three questions are necessary; none alone is sufficient.
Contributions. We make the following contributions:
1. Problem formalization: We define capability over-provisioning as a measurable security property (SER) and quantify it empirically on a live OpenClaw deployment.
2. AgentWarden framework: A four-layer adaptive governance system with a hybrid rule-based + fine-tuned LLM Safety Router (Layers 1, 3) and a PPO learning policy (Layer 2).

3. Empirical evaluation: Live deployment on OpenClaw v2026.3.28. Automated N=500 batch evaluation (400 benign + 100 adversarial, seed=42): 26.2% block rate, exec blocked 100%, 92% adversarial coverage. PPO achieves SER +260% (synthetic) and +337% (real sessions). 4. Critical finding: Tool-level governance is necessary but not sufficient -we document the first empirical demonstration of prompt injection succeeding at the LLM level but failing at the infrastructure level. 2 Related Work AI Agent Security. Agent security has emerged as a critical concern following the widespread adoption of autonomous agent runtimes. OWASP Foundation [2026] identified agentic skill supply chain attacks as a top-10 AI security risk, using ClawHavoc as the primary case study. Cisco AI Defense [2026] (Cisco, RSAC 2026) introduced DefenseClaw, which bundles skill scanning, MCP server verification, and code safety analysis into a single framework running inside NemoClaw's OpenShell runtime. DefenseClaw operates via static blocklists and anomaly detection -it does not learn or adapt per task type. NVIDIA [2026] (NVIDIA, GTC 2026) introduced NemoClaw with OpenShell, providing container-level isolation with declarative YAML policies for network, filesystem, and inference routing. Prompt Injection and Tool Misuse. Greshake et al. [2023] formalized indirect prompt injection in LLM-integrated applications. Perez and Ribeiro [2022] demonstrated that injected instructions reliably cause LLMs to deviate from their system prompts. Our work shows that even when prompt injection succeeds at the LLM level (causing the model to generate dangerous tool calls), infrastructure-level governance provides a hard enforcement boundary -a finding not previously demonstrated in the agent runtime context. Reinforcement Learning for Security Policy. Li et al. [2024] applied RL to adaptive network security policy, showing that learned policies outperform static rule sets for novel attack patterns. EmergentMind [2026] proposed curriculum-based agentic training with adaptive scheduling. Agent-Warden applies this principle at the infrastructure level -the RL policy learns optimal capability scoping without modifying the agent or LLM. Capability Control and Least Privilege. The principle of least privilege Saltzer and Schroeder [1975] underpins access control theory. arXiv [2026a] (EduClaw) applies agent-profile-based skill scaling in educational contexts. arXiv [2026b] proposes dual-stream continual skill learning in multimodal agents. Both operate at the model level; AgentWarden operates at the infrastructure level without model modification, making it runtime-agnostic.

div.head: LLM Tool-Calling Reliability.
div.p: Recent work has documented significant unreliability in LLM tool-calling: models hallucinate non-existent tools, invoke tools unnecessarily, and fail to terminate ReAct loops Qin et al. [2024]. This motivates infrastructure-level interception rather than relying on the model to self-govern. Our evaluation confirms this: qwen2.5:7b generated dangerous exec calls under adversarial prompting, while DeepSeek-chat refused at the model level -demonstrating that the optimal defense depends on the underlying model and that infrastructure governance provides a model-agnostic safety floor.
Positioning. Table 1 summarizes the key distinctions between AgentWarden and related systems.

div.head: The AgentWarden Framework
div.p: AgentWarden is a three-layer governance framework that operates above the AI agent runtime. It enforces the principle of least privilege by (i) restricting the agent's capability awareness before each session and (ii) intercepting every tool invocation before execution. The overall system architecture is illustrated in Figure 1.

div.head: Layer 1: Capability Governor
div.p: The Capability Governor enforces tool scoping at the semantic level: it controls which tools the agent is told it has, not just which it can execute. This is achieved through two mechanisms:

AGENTS.md injection. OpenClaw assembles a system prompt from workspace files, including AGENTS.md. The Governor generates a task-specific AGENTS.md that explicitly lists only the permitted tools: "This is a governed session scoped to summarization. 4 tools available: read, web fetch, memory search, memory get."

AgentWarden governance layer OpenClaw Gateway port 18789 • Docker Layer 1 -Capability Governor AGENTS.md injection • tools.deny • PPO policy (primary) • YAML fallback Layer 3 -Safety Router (MITM Proxy) Stage 1: rules Stage 2: agentwarden-router 0.1 ms ∼800 ms always block fine-tuned LLM Ollama • qwen2.5:7b port 11434 • GTX 1060 6 GB Audit DB (SQLite) router blocks • reward signals tools.deny injection. The Governor writes the denied tool list to openclaw.json (dynamically reloaded without gateway restart). This enforces the scope at the infrastructure level, ensuring the agent cannot invoke denied tools even if it reasons toward them.
The Governor accepts a TaskDescriptor and returns an AllowedCapabilitySet via a hybrid policy engine (Section 3.4).

div.head: Task Type: Definition and Classification
div.p: A task type τ ∈ T is a coarse semantic label over the agent's primary operation, determining the minimum viable capability set for a session. We define six types derived from the OpenClaw usage log (N=500 sessions): Summarisation, File Read, Web Research, Code Execution, Email, and Unknown. Each type maps to a minimum tool set; e.g., Summarization requires only {read, memory get, web search}, while Code Execution adds {write, edit} (full taxonomy in Appendix A).

Classification. Type is inferred from the agent's first user message by agentwarden-router (< 100 ms, confidence threshold 0.7). Sessions below threshold are assigned Unknown (≈12% of sessions), which uses a conservative read-only default. The Safety Router enforces rules regardless of task type. The Governor provides proactive scoping and the Router provides reactive enforcement. The current taxonomy is manually defined; automated induction from audit logs is identified as future work.

div.head: Layer 2: Safety Router
div.p: The Safety Router is a FastAPI MITM proxy deployed between OpenClaw and Ollama. It intercepts every POST /api/chat request, forwards it to Ollama, inspects the LLM response for tool calls, and classifies each call before OpenClaw can execute it. Block action. Blocked tool calls are stripped from the response; the agent receives: "AgentWarden blocked this tool call. The requested operation is not permitted in this governed session." Block events are logged to an SQLite audit database with reward signals for Layer 3 training.

div.head: Layer 3: RL Learning Policy
div.p: The RL policy learns the minimum viable tool set per task type from the accumulated audit log. This is the primary research contribution: the adaptive intelligence that static systems lack.

div.head: MDP formulation.
div.p: • State s: task type (one-hot, 6 types) ⊕ trust level (normalized ∈ [0, 1]); |s| = 7 • Action a: binary exposure mask over all 17 tools; a ∈ {0, 1} 17 (MultiBinary( 17)) • Reward: R(s, a) = α • U accuracy -β • C economy -γ • P safety where U accuracy ∈ {0, 1} is task success, C economy = 1 -SER penalises over-provisioning, and P safety counts Safety Router BLOCK events from the audit log. We set α = 1.0, β = 0.3, γ = 5.0.

Policy. PPO Schulman et al. [2017] with MlpPolicy (2 hidden layers, 64 units), trained via stable-baselines3 Raffin et al. [2021] on CPU. Trust-level hard constraints are applied postprediction: exec requires normalized trust ≥ 0.8 (i.e. trust level 4 on the raw 0-5 tenant scale), sessions spawn and subagents are never exposed regardless of policy output.
Integration. The trained policy (best model.zip) is loaded by the Governor's PolicyEngine as the primary decision maker. YAML rules serve as a fallback if the model file is unavailable.

div.head: Threat Model
div.p: AgentWarden defends against: (1) Prompt injection causing the agent to request dangerous tool calls; (2) Capability escalation via tools the agent should not have for the current task; (3) Subagent spawning for lateral movement; (4) Supply chain attacks via malicious skills (blocked by the Governor before skills are exposed to the agent).

AgentWarden does not govern the semantic content of agent responses -a model that expresses dangerous advice in text rather than tool calls is outside this system's scope (Section 5). 2 summarizes results across all evaluation phases, from baseline measurement through RL policy training.

div.head: N=500 Automated Batch Evaluation
div.p: To establish statistical scale beyond the 20-task structured evaluation, we ran an automated batch of 500 tasks (seed=42): 400 benign, 100 adversarial. 500 tasks generated from a fixed taxonomy (seed=42): 400 benign, 100 adversarial. Of 447 tool calls intercepted: all exec (70) and sessions spawn (8) blocked 100% at 0.1 ms. Overall avg SER 0.053. A fine-tuned LLM classifier blocked ∼22 benign write operations (HTTP server scripts) -false positives caused by 95%/5% training imbalance, discussed in §5.

div.p: To attribute SER gains to individual components, we ablate the system by disabling each stage in turn (100 tasks, seed=99, Table 5). Results. AgentWarden maintains BU of 89.7% (-1.0 pp vs. baseline), demonstrating near-zero utility cost from governance. ASR is reduced by 1.4 pp overall, with the largest gain in Slack (-5.7 pp). The modest overall ASR reduction is expected: important instructions injects payload into tool outputs (malicious text in email or file content), whereas AgentWarden governs tool calls. These are complementary threat surfaces.

This result contextualises our N=20 adversarial evaluation (Section 3): AgentWarden achieves 100% block rate on tool-call attacks (exec, sessions spawn), while important instructions-style attacks operate at the LLM reasoning boundary. Stage 3 semantic output filter addresses this gap (Section 4.8). AgentWarden governed 2,070 tool calls during the defended evaluation at 340 ms average governance latency.

div.head: Multi-Runtime Platform Validation
div.p: To validate framework-agnostic middleware operation, we conducted structured governance tests across three agent runtimes using the production codebase (agentwarden-core).

All tests used Stage 1 rules + Stage 2 classifier, with Ollama or DeepSeek backends. Base model reliability as a confound. qwen2.5:7b demonstrated significant tool-calling unreliability: 7 calls to session status in a single task, 2 timeouts on complex tasks, and use of web search for local file operations. This is a model capability constraint, not an AgentWarden limitation. The 20-task evaluation represents a lower bound on governance effectiveness. We expect stronger results with capable tool-calling models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, Qwen3-Coder).

SER = 1.0 as an artifact of synthetic training. The PPO policy achieved SER = 1.0 (theoretical optimum) because the RL environment simulated tool usage as a fixed fraction of exposed tools. In production, agents may use unexpected tools for creative problem-solving, yielding lower but more realistic SER values. Real session data (collected via the 20-task protocol) will calibrate the RL environment for the camera-ready version.

PPO policy collapse in production testing. Both PPO checkpoints collapsed to single-tool policies (predicting only memory search for all task types) -a known artifact of SER-maximizing training in synthetic environments. Collapse detection is implemented; detected collapse triggers YAML fallback with sensible per-task defaults. Retraining on real session data is planned for camera-ready.

Creative attack vectors. The model attempted to read untrusted input.txt via web fetch file:// -a creative workaround that bypassed the intended read tool. The arg-pattern classifier caught this novel approach, validating the value of pattern-based defense in depth.
Limitations and future work. (1) The RL policy state space does not include user identity or historical session behavior; adding these may improve personalisation at the cost of privacy.
(2) The LLM classifier's 2,094 ms latency is acceptable for interactive sessions but may require optimization for high-throughput deployments.

(3) Phase 3 (NemoClaw integration): the NemoClawParser is implemented and the defense-in-depth architecture validated (Section 4.8). Live end-to-end testing is deferred pending NVIDIA NIM API availability (NemoClaw is in alpha, March 2026). Phase 4 (Mobile NPU Runtime) is planned. (4) The fine-tuned agentwarden-router model was trained on only 273 examples with a severely imbalanced 95%/5% BLOCK/ALLOW split. Without finetuning, the base Qwen2.5-1.5B model performs poorly on this task -it lacks the domain knowledge to distinguish legitimate agent tool calls (e.g., writing an HTTP server script) from dangerous ones (e.g., exec with shell injection). Fine-tuning is therefore not optional but required for acceptable precision. The current dataset is a minimal proof-of-concept; a production-quality classifier would require at minimum 2,000-5,000 balanced examples covering the full diversity of enterprise tool-call patterns. Collecting this data via Shadow Mode ( §5) is the primary path to a robust classifier.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We presented AgentWarden, a framework-agnostic governance middleware that intercepts tool calls from any agent framework without modifying agent code, enforcing least-privilege access via a PPO-trained policy that maps session context and inferred task type to a minimal permitted tool set.

Validated across three agent runtimes (OpenClaw, DeepAgents, Hermes) and on the AgentDojo benchmark (97 tasks, 949 injection cases), AgentWarden achieves 100% adversarial coverage on tool-call attacks with 0% error rate, maintains BU of 89.7% (-1.0 pp vs. undefended), and reduces ASR by 1.4 pp on important instructions attacks orthogonal to the governed layer.

The key insight is framing capability scoping as a learned optimization problem: the policy learns the minimum viable tool set per task type, turning a static firewall into an adaptive immune system. SER provides a reproducible metric (10.5× over baseline in real sessions). We release production code and an evaluation framework; future work includes RL retraining on real audit logs, NemoClaw live integration, and a USENIX Security submission.

div.head: C Stage 3 Semantic Output Filter
div.p: Stage 3 inspects the text content of LLM responses for dangerous natural language (e.g. reverse shell instructions, credential exfiltration commands). This closes the gap documented in §5: a request for a reverse shell caused qwen2.5:7b to return nc -l -p 4444 instructions without generating a tool call.
Implementation. Llama Guard 3 (Meta, 8B, Ollama v0.20.

7) is wired into proxy.py v0.3.0 at three intercept points: /v1/chat/completions, /api/chat, and the DeepSeek bridge. Disabled by default (adds ≈1 s latency); enabled via AETHELGARD SEMANTIC FILTER=true. Model is swappable via AETHELGARD SEMANTIC MODEL=<ollama-model>. Evaluation design: fixed corpus over live generation. Model non-determinism invalidates livegeneration Stage 3 evaluation: qwen2.5:7b produces dangerous text for a given adversarial prompt on some runs and refuses on others. Llama Guard 3 behaves correctly in both cases -blocking dangerous responses, passing safe ones. The correct methodology is a fixed corpus of captured dangerous outputs: S14 = Code Interpreter Abuse. S7 = Privacy (credential exfiltration). Detection rate: 4/4 (100%). FPR: 0/3 (0%). First call 12,829ms (Llama Guard 3 cold start on GPU); warm calls 782-1,387ms. For production deployment, Shadow Mode (AMARE enterprise tier) builds this corpus automatically from live sessions, enabling continuous threshold calibration against a tenant's actual model and prompt distribution.

div.p: Test environment. Ubuntu 22.04; NVIDIA GPU 6 GB VRAM; Ollama v0.20.7 with GPU inference; AgentWarden proxy in Docker (port 8000), connected to host Ollama via Docker bridge network (172.18.0.1:11434). Models: gemma4:e4b (9.6 GB), deepseek-chat (API), hermes3:8b (5 GB), qwen2.5:7b (4.7 GB), llama-guard3 (4.9 GB), agentwarden-router (986 MB).

div.head: Stage 3 live interception (new result).
div.p: A bind shell prompt to qwen2.5:7b generated natural language reverse shell instructions on attempt 2 of 3 (model non-determinism, as documented in §5). Llama Guard 3 blocked the response: category S14 (Code Interpreter Abuse), confidence = 0.95, latency = 10,498 ms cold GPU (≈ 1,000 ms warm GPU). This is the first live end-to-end Stage 3 interception reported for the production agentwarden-core codebase.

Stage 3 false positive (Hermes XML). Llama Guard 3 classified <tool call> XML tags as category S1 (Violent Crimes) -a false positive caused by the structured XML format. Resolution: Stage 3 is skipped for responses where message content contains <tool call> tags or where tool calls is non-empty and content is empty. Stage 3 correctly targets natural language only.

DeepAgents LocalShellBackend bypass (new empirical finding). During DeepAgents integration testing, shell commands executed via LocalShellBackend returned real host filesystem contents (ls -la /tmp) without generating any LLM tool call. This empirically confirms the threat model boundary: agent runtimes with local execution backends bypass LLM-layer governance. Mitigation: FilesystemBackend() disables local shell execution; all tool calls route through the LLM and are intercepted by AgentWarden.

Hybrid classifier. Classification uses a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 (Rule-based, 0.1ms): A deterministic classifier checks: (1) always-block tools (exec, sessions spawn, subagents); (2) argument-level dangerous patterns (e.g., rm -rf, file://, AWS metadata endpoints, SSH credential paths); (3) prompt injection patterns ("ignore previous instructions", DAN mode, etc.). Stage 2 (LLM-based, ∼800ms): If Stage 1 passes, the call is classified by agentwarden-router, a Qwen2.5-1.5B model fine-tuned on 273 labeled block/allow examples collected from live sessions. The LLM stage is skipped for known-safe tools (read, memory search, web search) to avoid false positives.

div.p: A.1 Task Type Taxonomy Task taxonomy (N=500 batch eval). Tasks were generated from a fixed taxonomy with seed=42: 400 benign across 4 categories (summarisation, file read, web research, code execution) and 100 adversarial across 3 categories (prompt injection, DAN-mode variants, credential/tool exfiltration). Each task maps to a known minimum tool set, enabling U accuracy computation per Table 9. The 0.053 is the uncontrolled SER -how few tools the agent invokes when given all 17. The 0.557 is the governed SER under PPO. The +337% improvement is the ratio.

Classifier test set. The 11-case classifier evaluation in §4.2 is a smoke test. For camera-ready we construct a balanced held-out set of n ≥ 200 from the N=500 audit log (117 BLOCK + 117 matched ALLOW decisions, plus 20 OOD adversarial examples not in training distribution). The extraction script (scripts/extract classifier testset.py) and resulting JSONL are released openly under CC BY 4.0. Adversarial breakdown (N=500). Of 100 adversarial tasks: 38 blocked by Safety Router (infrastructure), 54 refused by model (DeepSeek-chat safety training), 8 benign-intent adversarial prompts that generated no dangerous tool calls and correctly passed. Attack success rate: 0/100. The 8 textonly cases are outside AgentWarden's defined scope (capability governance, not content filtering).
